content:
A product photography brief for an online store should fix the number and order of images each product needs, the file specifications, a consistent style and a naming and upload routine, before anyone picks up a camera. For ecommerce website development in Pune, this is the work that most often gets left until the end and then rushed: the site is ready, the catalogue is entered, and the photographs arrive in different sizes, backgrounds and orientations, so the store looks unfinished however good the design is. This guide gives you a shot list by product type, practical image specifications for Shopify and WooCommerce stores, a consistency checklist, a workflow for handling hundreds of products, and a brief you can give to a photographer or an in-house team.

It is written for owners of Pune retail, D2C and wholesale businesses who are building or rebuilding an online store, and for the developers and photographers who work with them. We do not quote photography prices, because they depend on the product, the number of images and the studio; ask for a written per-image or per-product rate and what it includes. We also avoid claims that a particular number of images raises sales by a particular amount. The reasoning below comes from how shoppers use product pages, and you should test it on your own store.

## Why Product Images Are Website Work, Not Just Photography

A customer cannot touch the product. Images carry the job that a shop assistant does in a physical store: showing the size, the colour, the texture, how it is used and what is included in the box. If the pictures are unclear, the shopper asks the questions that the page should have answered, or leaves.

Images are also a technical matter. They are usually the heaviest part of a product page, so their format and dimensions affect loading speed, which we discuss in our guides to [image optimisation with AVIF and WebP](/blog/website-designer-pune-image-optimization-avif-webp-lcp-2026) and to [store speed and Core Web Vitals](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-store-speed-core-web-vitals-2026). They feed Google Search, Google Shopping and Meta catalogue ads, each with its own image rules. And they must be consistent across hundreds of products, which is a process problem. That is why we treat the brief as part of the build.

## Step One: Decide What Each Product Page Needs to Show

Start from the questions a buyer has, not from what is easy to photograph. For every product, a good set answers these.

1. What does it look like? (the main image)
2. How big is it? (a scale reference or a person)
3. What do the details look like up close? (material, stitching, finish, ports)
4. How is it used? (an in-context or lifestyle image)
5. What is included? (all items laid out)
6. What are the variants? (each colour, pattern or finish)

### A shot list by product type

| Product type | Core shots | Useful extras |
|---|---|---|
| Clothing and textiles | Front, back, side, detail of fabric, on-model | Flat lay, size chart image, movement video |
| Jewellery | Clean front view, close-up macro, worn | Scale against a hand, packaging |
| Home and kitchen | Main view, in-use, dimensions diagram | Box contents, size comparison |
| Electronics | Front, ports and controls, box contents | Screen on, in-use, accessories |
| Food and packaged goods | Front of pack, back of pack with label, serving | Ingredients close-up, hamper contents |
| Furniture | Front, side, detail, in a room | Dimensions diagram, assembly view |
| Industrial and B2B | Product on plain background, label, scale | Installation view, certifications |

For food and packaged goods, remember that the label itself is information buyers and regulators care about. Make sure the back-of-pack photo is sharp enough to read. If your listing shows weights, ingredients or other legal details, take them from the real label and keep them current. Our article on [legal metrology rules](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-legal-metrology-rules-2026) covers what an ecommerce listing must show.

### How many images?

There is no magic number. Many stores aim for four to eight images for a typical product and more for complex or high-value items, but let the questions above decide. A simple stainless-steel bottle may need four. A sofa needs more. Beware of adding images only to reach a count; each image should answer something.

## Step Two: Technical Specifications to Put in the Brief

### Dimensions and aspect ratio

Choose one aspect ratio for the main product images and keep to it across the catalogue. Square (1:1) is the most common and works well in grids and in marketplace and ad feeds. Some fashion stores use 4:5 or 3:4 portrait. Whatever you choose, shoot with room around the product so that you can crop for other uses.

Shoot and supply originals larger than the size shown on the site, so that zooming and different layouts work. Check your platform's guidance, since it changes. Shopify's help pages publish a recommended maximum and recommended dimensions for product images; WooCommerce uses the image sizes defined by the theme and lets you regenerate thumbnails. Ask your developer which sizes the theme generates, and supply originals at least as large as the biggest one.

### Requirements from Google and Meta

If you plan to list products on Google (free listings and Shopping ads through Merchant Center) or run Meta catalogue ads, their rules for the main image apply. As of our last reading of Google's Merchant Center help, they included these points; confirm the current text before you shoot, because the rules are updated.

- The image should show the product itself, with no promotional text, watermarks or placeholder images.
- The image must be large enough: minimum dimensions are specified (larger for apparel) and a maximum file size applies.
- The product should fill most of the frame, on a plain or neutral background for the main image.

Meta's catalogue guidance similarly asks for high-quality images that show the product, with a minimum resolution and a preference for square ratios. Our guide to [Meta catalogue ads, product feeds and the pixel](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-meta-catalog-ads-product-feed-pixel-2026) and the article on [Google Merchant Center](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-google-merchant-center-2026) show how the feed uses the main image and the additional images separately.

### File formats and size

- Supply originals as high-quality JPEG or PNG (or the camera's raw files kept as masters). The store or its image service should convert to WebP or AVIF for delivery.
- Use PNG or a transparent format only when you need transparency; photographs are far smaller as JPEG.
- Embed an sRGB colour profile so that colours are predictable across devices.
- Keep each delivered web image to a size your developer approves. Compression should be tuned so that images look sharp but load quickly; a heavy 5 MB photo on a product page is a performance problem on a mobile connection.

### File names and alt text

Name files so that humans and systems can sort them: a consistent pattern like `sku-colour-view-01.jpg` (for example, `BTL-1L-STEEL-front-01.jpg`). This lets a developer bulk-upload and match images to products by SKU, as described in our guide to [product catalogue data preparation](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-product-catalogue-data-preparation-2026).

Alt text is part of the page, not decoration. Write a short, honest description of what the image shows ("Steel 1-litre bottle, front view, matte blue"). Do not stuff it with keywords. Alt text serves screen-reader users and appears when an image fails to load. Google's image guidance treats it as helpful context about the image.

## Step Three: Make the Set Look Like One Shop

A catalogue of good photos can still look amateur if they differ from each other. Consistency is what separates a store that feels trustworthy from a collection of snapshots.

### The consistency checklist

- **Background:** one colour or treatment for main images (white or light grey is typical). Lifestyle images can differ, but within a theme.
- **Lighting:** the same direction, softness and colour temperature. Shadows treated the same way.
- **Angle and framing:** the same angle for the same product type, the product filling a similar proportion of the frame.
- **Scale:** products shot to a consistent apparent size where possible.
- **Colour accuracy:** the colour on screen matches the product. Returns for "colour not as shown" are an avoidable cost.
- **Retouching:** remove dust and scratches; do not alter shape, colour or features, which would mislead customers.
- **Order of images:** the same sequence on every product (front, side, back, detail, in-use).

Create a reference sheet for the photographer: three or four example images that set the standard, with notes. Review the first ten products before the studio shoots the other hundred. Catching a framing problem on product ten is cheap; on product 400 it is not.

### Honest representation

Images must not mislead. Show the actual product that will arrive, with accurate colour, correct size relative to the scale reference, and everything included in the price. If the photograph shows accessories that are not included, label it. India's Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 and the guidelines on misleading advertisements require sellers to describe goods accurately, and a mismatch between image and product is a common cause of complaints and returns. For the wider legal context, see our article on [consumer protection rules for ecommerce](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-consumer-protection-rules-2026).

## Step Four: Video and Other Formats

Short videos can answer questions that still images cannot: how a garment moves, how a gadget operates, how large a bag really is. Keep them short, silent-friendly (many people watch on mute) and hosted so that they do not slow the page. A few notes.

- Show the product in use and from several angles within 15 to 30 seconds.
- Provide captions or text on screen for key points.
- Use a poster image and load the video only when the visitor chooses to play it, or lazy-load it, so that the page speed does not suffer.
- Do not autoplay with sound.

Other useful formats are a 360-degree spin for products where shape matters, a size-and-fit image for clothing (see our article on [size charts, variants and fit guides](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-size-charts-variants-fit-guides-2026)), and a short "what is in the box" image.

## Step Five: A Workflow That Scales to Hundreds of Products

Photographing five products is a creative task. Photographing five hundred is a production line, and the process decides whether the launch is on time.

1. **Build the product list first,** with SKU, name and variants, and decide who owns it. The list drives shot planning.
2. **Group products by type and shoot in batches,** so lighting and set-up stay the same.
3. **Label every product physically** with its SKU before shooting, so the images can be matched later.
4. **Shoot a test product** and run it through the full path to a live test page, to check cropping, size and loading before the main shoot.
5. **Edit in batches** with the same presets, and export at the agreed sizes.
6. **Name files by the agreed pattern** and place them in a shared folder with one subfolder per product or per batch.
7. **Upload in bulk** using the platform's import tools, matching by SKU, or let a developer script it. Check a sample of products on a phone and desktop.
8. **Keep the originals** in organised storage with a backup. You will need them for new layouts, marketplaces and ads.

A common cause of launch delays is images arriving late, so plan the photography into the project timeline. Our guide to [why website projects are delayed by content](/blog/web-development-company-pune-website-content-copy-photos-launch-delays-2026) explains the pattern, and the [pre-launch testing checklist](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-pre-launch-testing-checklist-2026) includes an image check.

## In-House, Freelance or Studio?

| Option | Suits | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| In-house with a light box and a phone or camera | Small catalogues of small, simple items; frequent new products | Inconsistent lighting, time taken from other work |
| Freelance photographer | Mid-sized catalogues, a one-off shoot | Availability, style consistency across sessions, who owns the files |
| Product photography studio | Large catalogues, difficult products (jewellery, glass, apparel on models) | Cost, turnaround time, minimum order |

A good phone camera and a simple lighting set-up can produce acceptable main images of small products, if the discipline of background, lighting and framing is held. Difficult materials (reflective jewellery, glass, black products) and on-model fashion usually repay professional help. Whichever route you choose, agree in writing on the number of images per product, the specifications above, the turnaround time, the number of revision rounds, who owns the images and where they will be stored. If you are choosing a photographer, ask for samples of consistent catalogue work, not only portfolio highlights.

Govindani Infotech offers [product photography](/services/product-shoot) and [photography services](/services/photography) alongside website development, so that shoot specifications and the store's image requirements are planned together. Whether you use us or another team, the brief below applies.

## The Brief: A Template to Copy

Give your photographer or team this, filled in for your store.

1. **Products:** the list with SKUs, variants and the priority order.
2. **Shot list per product type:** the images in the order required.
3. **Aspect ratio and size:** for example, square, minimum pixel dimensions, original files supplied.
4. **Background and style:** reference images and notes.
5. **Colour and retouching rules:** accurate colour, sRGB, no shape changes.
6. **File format and names:** the pattern and an example.
7. **Delivery:** folder structure, deadline, number of revision rounds.
8. **Rights:** who owns the images, whether they may be used by the photographer in a portfolio, and for how long.
9. **Special handling:** fragile items, food hygiene, branded packaging.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How many photos should each product have on an online store?
There is no fixed number. Most products need enough images to answer the buyer's questions: appearance, size, detail, use and what is included. Four to eight suffices for many items, with more for complex or expensive products. Add an image only if it answers something.

### What size should product images be for Shopify or WooCommerce?
Use one consistent aspect ratio, often square, and supply originals larger than the biggest size shown so that zoom works. Check the platform's current guidance and your theme's image sizes. Let the store or an image service deliver compressed WebP or AVIF versions.

### Can I use my phone to photograph products?
Yes, for small, simple products, provided you use even lighting, a plain background, a steady mount and the same set-up every time. Reflective or dark products and on-model fashion generally need more skill and equipment.

### Do product images affect SEO and Google Shopping?
They can affect how your listings appear in image search and Shopping, and large images slow the page if not optimised. Google Merchant Center has rules for main images, such as no watermarks or promotional text, so check the current requirements before you shoot.

### Who should own the product photographs?
Normally you, the business that commissions them. Agree this in writing, including whether the photographer may reuse them, and keep your own backup of the original files.

## Where to Start

Pick your five best-selling products and write a shot list for each from the buyer's questions. Shoot just those five to the specifications above, upload them to a test page on your store, and view them on a phone. The problems you meet, such as slow loading, awkward crops or colours that do not match, are the problems you would have met 500 times, and the brief is easy to correct at this stage.
